what_it_does: A Physical Unclonable Function (PUF) is a hardware security primitive that exploits tiny, uncontrollable manufacturing variations in a chip to generate a unique fingerprint — like a chip's DNA — used for authentication without storing a secret key. ReRAM-based PUFs use resistance variations in resistive memory cells as the source of randomness, but those variations can shift with temperature or electrical noise, making the fingerprint unreliable. They are also vulnerable to machine-learning modeling attacks (where an attacker trains a neural network on many challenge-response pairs to predict the PUF's future responses) and side-channel attacks (where an attacker monitors power consumption or timing to infer the secret). Re4PUF uses a 3T2R cell (three transistors, two resistive elements) with a digitally adjustable voltage supply to stabilize responses against temperature and noise, and allows the circuit to be reconfigured cheaply by tweaking voltages — without re-writing the resistive elements — so that a known challenge-response mapping can be invalidated after an attack attempt.
